df213d54-e468-4c35-962c-20576d558c00.text: Compare how personal loss is presented in Poppies and Cousin Kate. You should compare language, form and structure, and consider contexts. [20 marks]
df213d54-e468-4c35-962c-20576d558c00.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Both poems are voiced by women experiencing loss — Weir's mother losing her son to war, Rossetti's speaker losing her status and innocence to a lord's exploitation. Weir uses free verse and enjambment to mirror uncontrolled emotion; Rossetti uses ballad form to place her story in a folk tradition of wronged women. Both use physical imagery: Weir's textile metaphor (pinning, smoothing) vs Rossetti's possessive similes ('wore me like a silken knot'). Weir's modern context (Remembrance, mothers of serving soldiers) vs Rossetti's Victorian context (sexual double standards, women as property).
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Limited.

Top band (21-25): Perceptive contextual analysis. Discusses: published 2010 (pre-marriage equality); homophobic bullying in British schools a real and present reality; teenage parenthood; masculine norms and emotional suppression. Blackman's role as a writer committed to stories young people need — and her later appointment as Children's Laureate (2013-2015). Comments on the novel's refusal to offer false comfort: Adam is not safe because he is open; the family is not healed; Josh's accountability is not redemption.
Top band (16-20): Clear contextual discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant points.

f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.text: Compare how Nichols and Hood use form and structure to present different experiences of belonging. You should consider the poets' use of language, form and structure, as well as the contexts in which the poems were written. [20 marks]
f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive comparison. Analyses Nichols's free verse, enjambment and lack of punctuation (dreamlike, fluid identity) against Hood's regular stanza pattern and refrain (orderly grief, contained loss). Caribbean migration vs Victorian nostalgia. Connects form to meaning throughout.
Top band (13-16): Sustained comparison with clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Clear comparison with some analysis of form.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.text: How does Chingonyi's use of the Luvale language in the title 'Kumukanda' contribute to the poem's exploration of identity? [10 marks]
f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.marks:
Top band (9-10) Perceptive analysis. Explores the title as code-switching, cultural reclamation, and the gap between naming heritage (Luvale) and explaining it (English). British-Zambian identity, diaspora.
Top band (7-8): Sustained analysis.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear explanation.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comment.

f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.text: Explain how the use of free verse in 'Island Man' reflects the speaker's experience of dual identity.
f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Identifies free verse with enjambment and minimal punctuation (1 mark)
- Explains that the flowing lines mirror the blurring of Caribbean and London worlds (1 mark)
- Analyses how the absence of traditional form reflects an identity that refuses to be contained (1 mark)
- Links to Caribbean migrant experience, living between two cultures (1 mark)

f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.text: Compare how two poems from the Belonging collection use contrasting forms to express different attitudes to belonging. [20 marks]
f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive comparison of form. Analyses how one Romantic poem's regular structure expresses certainty against a contemporary poem's free verse expressing uncertainty. Integrates AO2 (specific techniques) and AO3 (context explaining why forms differ).
Top band (13-16): Developed comparison.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.text: Analyse how Bridges's regular rhyme scheme in 'Clear and Gentle Stream' reinforces the poem's themes.
f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Identifies the regular, predictable rhyme scheme (1 mark)
- Explains that it mirrors the steady, reliable flow of the stream (1 mark)
- Analyses how regularity conveys nature's constancy and the speaker's sense of stable belonging (1 mark)
- Contrasts with contemporary free verse poets whose irregular forms reflect uncertain belonging (1 mark)

f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.text: Explore how enjambment is used differently in 'Island Man' and 'Us' to convey ideas about belonging. [10 marks]
f9cd74de-d36c-4acc-a3ca-cf96075bdc59.marks:
Top band (9-10) Perceptive analysis. Explores Nichols's enjambment as dreamlike flow between two worlds vs Kunial's as stretching meaning across lines, forcing reinterpretation of words. Both use enjambment to reflect identities that do not fit neatly into single categories.
Top band (7-8): Sustained analysis.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear explanation.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some points.

5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.text: How does Blackman present the homophobic attack and its aftermath as the central crisis of the novel? You should consider the context in which the novel was written.
5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of the attack as a structural and thematic climax. Discusses: the engineering by Logan, Josh's role as Adam's former boyfriend, Adam's hospitalisation, Dante's report to police, Adam's depression and suicidal crisis. Context: homophobic violence in early 21st-century Britain, Blackman's refusal to soften the aftermath. Comments on the novel's structural convergence of the two storylines.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.text: Explore how Blackman uses Josh's participation in the attack to develop the theme of internalised homophobia.
5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive thematic analysis. Discusses: Josh as Adam's secret boyfriend and his attacker — the central irony; Logan's engineering of the attack as a test; Josh's choice of violence over vulnerability; his eventual confession and turn-in to police. Context: peer pressure, masculinity, shame. Blackman's argument that internalised homophobia destroys the person who carries it as well as the person it targets.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited points.

5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.text: "Blackman refuses to allow the reader an easy recovery narrative." How does the novel's treatment of Adam's aftermath support this view?
5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive discussion of narrative honesty. Discusses: hospitalisation, depression, withdrawal, suicidal ideation — the full arc of trauma rather than a shortcut to resilience. How this choice deepens the novel's moral seriousness. Blackman's refusal to sentimentalise or minimise the consequences of violence. Context: mental health, the long effects of hate crime.
Top band (16-20): Clear argument.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant discussion.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.text: How does Blackman present Dante's response to the attack, and what does his behaviour reveal about his character?
5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of Dante's moral choices. Discusses: physical restraint preventing him intervening; reporting to police and naming his friends as attackers; the parallel with journalism — Dante tells the truth at great personal cost. His protectiveness towards Adam as evidence of the growth he has undergone through fatherhood. His decision to report as moral clarity.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.text: How does Blackman use the resolution of the novel to suggest that resilience is possible but hard-won?
5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of resolution. Discusses: Adam's recovery as slow, not triumphant; Dante embracing rather than enduring fatherhood; the family's movement towards greater openness; Josh's accountability as partial acknowledgement. The novel's refusal of easy happiness alongside its insistence that survival is possible. Context: resilience, recovery, the possibility of change.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.text: Explore how Blackman presents peer pressure as a force that shapes male behaviour in the novel.
5e1f7a3d-faf5-456c-b400-275a930bc87e.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive contextual analysis. Discusses: Logan engineering the attack as a test; Josh unable to resist peer pressure even when it requires violence against someone he cares about; the social world of Dante's friend group as one in which homophobia is tolerated and even weaponised. Context: masculinity norms, group identity, moral courage under social pressure. Blackman's argument that silence and complicity are forms of participation.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant analysis.

0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.text: Compare how the poets present attitudes towards authority in The Charge of the Light Brigade and one other poem from the Conflict anthology. [20 marks]
0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Strong choices: Half-caste (challenging racial authority), Cousin Kate (challenging patriarchal authority), What Were They Like? (challenging military/political authority). Analyses Tennyson's dual attitude — celebrating soldiers' obedience ('Theirs not to reason why') while criticising command ('Someone had blundered'). Comparison poem analysed with equivalent depth. AO3 woven throughout: Tennyson's role as Poet Laureate, context of comparison poem.

0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.text: Compare how the poets present the power of nature in Extract from The Prelude and one other poem from the Conflict anthology. [20 marks]
0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Strong choice: Exposure (nature as hostile enemy). Analyses Wordsworth's personification ('Strode after me') and blank verse creating awe vs Owen's personification ('merciless iced east winds') and half-rhyme creating dread. Explores how Wordsworth's nature is sublime and educational (the boy learns humility) vs Owen's nature is brutally lethal (soldiers die from cold). Romantic sublime vs WW1 realism.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Limited.

0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.text: From memory, write three quotations from your best-prepared poem. For each, identify the technique and explain the effect.
0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.marks:
Top band (7-8): Three accurate quotations, each with a precisely identified technique and a detailed explanation of effect. E.g. for Exposure: 1. 'merciless iced east winds that knive us' — personification; nature is weaponised, suggesting the soldiers' greatest enemy is the weather. 2. 'But nothing happens' — refrain; creates crushing futility through repetition. 3. 'Slowly our ghosts drag home' — metaphor; the soldiers are psychologically dead even before they die physically.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Three quotations with clear technique + effect.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Two quotations or limited analysis.

0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.text: Compare how the poets present loss and grief in Poppies and Cousin Kate. You should compare language, form and structure, and consider contexts. [20 marks]
0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Both speakers are women experiencing profound loss — Weir's mother losing a son to war, Rossetti's speaker losing innocence and status to exploitation. Weir's free verse and enjambment mirror uncontrolled emotion; Rossetti's ballad form places her in a folk tradition of wronged women. Weir's textile imagery ('pinned', 'crimped') connects domestic and military worlds; Rossetti's possessive similes ('wore me like a glove') reduce the speaker to an object. modern vs Victorian contexts; different social constraints on women's expression of grief.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Limited.

0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.text: Write a 5-minute exam plan for: 'Compare how the poets present the reality of violence in Belfast Confetti and one other poem.' Include: chosen poem, 4 comparison points, key quotations, and one AO3 point per poem.
0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.marks:
Top band (7-8): Complete plan with all elements. E.g. Chosen poem: The Destruction of Sennacherib. Points: 1. Both present destruction, but Carson's is chaotic/urban, Byron's is divine/absolute. 2. Carson's fragmented form vs Byron's driving AABB couplets. 3. Carson's punctuation-as-shrapnel metaphor vs Byron's colour imagery (purple/gold → pale/chill). 4. Carson's unanswered questions vs Byron's certain, resolved narrative. Quotations: 'raining exclamation marks' (Carson), 'like the wolf on the fold' (Byron). Carson — the Troubles, personal experience; Byron — biblical source, Romantic fascination with power.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear plan with most elements.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Partial plan.

0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.text: A student has 5 minutes left in the exam. What should they prioritise: writing another paragraph, or proofreading their existing response? Explain your answer with reference to the mark scheme.
0adf4076-69f4-40e2-ab8b-33e77de8dccc.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- If they have only 3-4 paragraphs, another paragraph adds more AO2 evidence and potentially a new comparison point (1 mark)
- If they have 4-5 paragraphs already, proofreading is more valuable — checking every paragraph compares both poems, checking terminology is used, checking quotations are accurate (1 mark)
- credit goes to sustained comparison and precise analysis over quantity — 4 strong paragraphs beat 6 weak ones (1 mark)
- Quick proofreading wins: add a comparison connective where one is missing, correct a misremembered quotation, add a context sentence (1 mark)

df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.text: Analyse how Agard uses the examples of Picasso and Tchaikovsky to challenge the term 'half-caste' in Half-caste.
df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Agard asks if mixing red and green on a canvas makes a 'half-caste canvas' — exposing the absurdity of calling a person 'half' (1 mark)
- The Tchaikovsky example (black key + white key = 'half-caste symphony') applies the same logic to music, showing the term is ridiculous in any context (1 mark)
- By choosing celebrated art and music, Agard implies that mixing produces something beautiful and complete, not something lesser (1 mark)
- Links to his wider argument: the label diminishes a whole person, and the examples force the reader to see how illogical and dehumanising it is (1 mark)

df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.text: How does Carson use punctuation as a metaphor in Belfast Confetti? Refer to specific examples and analyse the effect on the reader.
df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Discusses 'raining exclamation marks' as punctuation becoming shrapnel — language itself is weaponised and fragmented by violence. Analyses the dashes that interrupt the speaker's thoughts ('I know this labyrinth so well —') as mimicking how violence disrupts normal life. Explores the unanswered questions at the end ('What is / My name?') as showing identity itself has been shattered. The poem's form enacts its meaning: broken sentences reflect a broken city.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of punctuation as metaphor.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some identification of the technique.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.text: Compare how social prejudice is challenged in Half-caste and The Class Game. You should compare language, form and structure, and consider relevant contexts. [20 marks]
df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Both poets reject standard English conventions as an act of resistance — Agard uses Caribbean dialect, Casey uses working-class dialect. Both use direct address to confront the listener/reader. Agard uses satire and absurd examples (Picasso, Tchaikovsky); Casey uses listing to catalogue class markers (deck chair vs yacht). Agard's Guyanese-British identity vs Casey's working-class British identity; both face prejudice based on how they speak. Key difference: Agard addresses racial categorisation, Casey addresses class snobbery.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison, limited analysis.
Lower band (1-5): Mostly descriptive.

df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.text: How does Zephaniah use repetition and rhythm in No Problem to challenge racism? You should consider the whole poem.
df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The refrain 'I am not de problem' is both a denial of blame and an assertion of identity — it turns the accusation back on the accuser. The dub rhythm (reggae-influenced, musical cadence) makes the poem performative — protest becomes art and celebration. The humour ('I am born academic') refuses to be defined by stereotypes. Zephaniah as a dub poet in the Jamaican-British oral tradition.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of repetition and rhythm.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant observations.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.text: Analyse how the final questions in Belfast Confetti ('What is / My name? Where am I coming from? Where am I going?') convey the impact of violence on identity.
df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- The questions address the most fundamental aspects of identity: name, origin, destination — all stripped away by violence (1 mark)
- They are left unanswered, reflecting the speaker's inability to think clearly in the aftermath of an explosion (1 mark)
- The line break in 'What is / My name?' physically fragments the question, mirroring the fragmentation of the speaker's mind (1 mark)
- Links to the Troubles context: in Belfast, identity (Catholic/Protestant, nationalist/unionist) was a matter of life and death, making these questions existentially dangerous (1 mark)

df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.text: Explore how Casey uses the structure of The Class Game to build her argument against class prejudice. Consider her use of listing, direct address and contrast.
df73b4ea-fef5-4400-bb56-b679ba058904.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The listing technique builds an overwhelming catalogue of class markers — each pair (deck chair/yacht, corgi/whippet) exposes how trivial and arbitrary the differences are. Direct address ('How can you tell?') makes the reader complicit — they are forced to examine their own assumptions. The contrasts between working-class and middle-class details are presented without hierarchy, implying neither is superior. Casey's working-class identity means the poem speaks from experience, not theory.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some observations about structure.
Lower band (1-2): Simple description.

76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.text: Analyse how Byron uses the simile 'like the wolf on the fold' in the opening of The Destruction of Sennacherib.
76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- 'Wolf' presents the Assyrian army as predatory, aggressive and dangerous (1 mark)
- 'Fold' refers to a flock of sheep — the Israelites are presented as vulnerable and defenceless (1 mark)
- The simile establishes the power imbalance: a mighty predator vs helpless prey, which makes the subsequent divine destruction even more dramatic (1 mark)
- Links to the biblical context: God defends the weak against the powerful, overturning the expected outcome (1 mark)

76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.text: How does Clarke present the conflict of motherhood in Catrin? You should consider language, form and structure.
76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The 'tight / Red rope of love' (umbilical cord) is both a bond and a battleground — 'rope' suggests tug-of-war rather than tenderness. The two-stanza structure mirrors two stages: physical separation at birth and emotional separation as the child grows. 'First fierce confrontation' uses alliteration to stress intensity. The present-tense 'Still I am fighting / You off' shows the conflict is ongoing — motherhood is a perpetual negotiation between holding on and letting go.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding of the mother-daughter conflict.
Lower band (1-2): Simple description.

76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.text: Compare how destruction is presented in The Destruction of Sennacherib and Belfast Confetti. You should compare language, form and structure, and consider relevant contexts. [20 marks]
76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained, convincing comparison. Byron's destruction is divine, ordered and absolute — AABB couplets and anapaestic rhythm drive relentlessly forward. Carson's is human, chaotic and random — fragmented free verse mirrors a bomb blast. Byron's colour imagery tracks from life (purple/gold) to death (pale/still); Carson's punctuation metaphor shows language itself shattering. Byron retells a biblical story to celebrate divine power; Carson writes from personal experience of the Troubles to convey its psychological impact.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with some analysis of methods.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison, limited analysis.
Lower band (1-5): Mostly descriptive.

76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.text: How does Byron use the anapaestic metre in The Destruction of Sennacherib to convey the experience of the cavalry charge?
76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- The anapaestic rhythm (da-da-DUM, da-da-DUM) creates a galloping, energetic beat that mimics horses charging (1 mark)
- The regularity of the metre gives the poem a relentless, unstoppable momentum — like the army itself (1 mark)
- This energy makes the sudden destruction more dramatic: the same rhythm that conveyed power now conveys collapse (1 mark)
- Links to the poem's narrative arc: the driving rhythm carries the reader from the army's arrival through to its annihilation without pause (1 mark)

76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.text: Explore how Clarke uses the symbol of the 'red rope of love' throughout Catrin. How does this single image capture the poem's central conflict?
76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The 'rope' is the umbilical cord — literally connecting mother and child. 'Red' connotes blood, passion and danger, suggesting the bond is intense and visceral. 'Love' softens the imagery, but 'rope' also suggests restraint, tug-of-war and bondage. The oxymoronic quality captures the poem's core truth: the mother-child relationship is simultaneously loving and combative. The rope is physically cut at birth but emotionally persists — 'Still I am fighting / You off' — showing separation is never complete.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of the symbol.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding of the metaphor.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.text: How does Byron use colour imagery in The Destruction of Sennacherib to chart the shift from power to death? Refer to specific quotations.
76400dfa-4462-4ea0-a916-cf1c29f1b6e4.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. 'Purple and gold' in the opening connote royalty, wealth and military splendour. The army's 'cohorts gleaming' suggests they are dazzling and magnificent. By the morning, the soldiers' eyes are 'deadly and chill' — warmth has been replaced by cold. The 'widows of Ashur are loud in their wail' shifts focus from the army's glory to human grief. The colour journey (vibrant → pale → absent) parallels the journey from life to death, from power to oblivion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of colour shift.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some identification of colour imagery.
Lower band (1-2): Basic observations.

175d5a2f-60ea-4fdc-9897-72ed6417b50c.text: Compare how the poets present attitudes to place in 'London' by Blake and one other poem from the Time and Place collection. In your answer you should compare the poets' use of language, form and structure and the influence of contexts on the poems. [20 marks]
175d5a2f-60ea-4fdc-9897-72ed6417b50c.marks:

Blake: 'charter'd' (control, commercialisation), anaphora of 'every' (universality), 'mind-forg'd manacles' (psychological oppression), tight quatrains (controlled rage). Comparison poem analysed with equal depth. Integrated structure using comparative connectives. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained with clear analysis. Mid band (7-9) Clear comparison. Lower-mid band (4-6) Some relevant comment. Lower band (1-3) Simple.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Perceptive contextual links for both poems. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some. Lower-mid band (2) Limited. Lower band (1) Simple.

175d5a2f-60ea-4fdc-9897-72ed6417b50c.text: Compare how the poets present the power of the natural world in 'To Autumn' by Keats and one other poem from the Time and Place collection. [20 marks]
175d5a2f-60ea-4fdc-9897-72ed6417b50c.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison. Keats: sensory imagery ('mellow fruitfulness'), personification, ode form, acceptance. Strong comparison with Dickinson (sea as threatening 'He,' hymn metre) or Davidson (organ metaphor, impersonal grandeur). Explores different relationships between humans and nature. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained. Mid band (7-9) Clear. Lower-mid band (4-6) Some. Lower band (1-3) Simple.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Perceptive — Romantic values, Keats's mortality, comparison poet's context. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some.

175d5a2f-60ea-4fdc-9897-72ed6417b50c.text: Compare how the poets present feelings of displacement in 'Presents from my Aunts in Pakistan' by Alvi and one other poem from the Time and Place collection. [20 marks]
175d5a2f-60ea-4fdc-9897-72ed6417b50c.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison. Alvi: colour imagery (vivid Pakistani vs plain English), 'of no fixed nationality,' free verse in seven uneven stanzas. Strong comparison with Nichols (pronoun shift, epizeuxis, resolution) or Adcock (precise observation, outsider status). Analyses how methods create different emotional outcomes. c25f6db3-84f3-436c-bfbc-cf5a1fdc57e5.marks:

Sherriff uses this gap to foreshadow Raleigh’s loss of innocence and to highlight how the war has changed Stanhope.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Raleigh is excited.

c25f6db3-84f3-436c-bfbc-cf5a1fdc57e5.text: Explain how the dugout setting contributes to the mood and themes of Act 1.
c25f6db3-84f3-436c-bfbc-cf5a1fdc57e5.marks:
Upper band (3-4): The cramped dugout creates claustrophobia and confinement. Characters cannot leave, mirroring the trapped feeling of trench warfare. The setting functions as a microcosm of the officers’ entire experience.

d65db752-979e-4192-9f80-d01ba8fa7dd8.text: Explore how Syal uses the economic decline of Tollington to explain the rise of racism in the novel.

0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.text: Analyse how Blake uses the extended metaphor of the tree to present the growth of anger in A Poison Tree.
0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Discusses how Blake maps the stages of anger onto the stages of plant growth: 'waterd it in fears' and 'sunned it with smiles' use nurturing language ironically for something toxic. The 'apple bright' alludes to the Garden of Eden, suggesting suppressed anger creates deadly temptation. The final image of the enemy 'outstretchd beneath the tree' parallels the Fall of Man — dishonesty leads to destruction. Links to Blake's critique of institutions that teach emotional repression.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant textual references.

0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.text: How does Wordsworth present the conflict between the boy and nature in the extract from The Prelude? Refer to specific language and structural choices.
0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Explores the shift from joy ('lustily I dipped my oars') to terror ('with trembling oars'). Analyses personification of the mountain ('Strode after me', 'measured motion like a living thing') as nature becoming a conscious, threatening presence. Discusses blank verse as mirroring the relentless, unbroken advance of the mountain. Notes that the aftermath ('huge and mighty forms') shows the experience permanently altering the boy's psychology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of the boy's changing emotions.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant observations.

0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.text: Analyse how Rossetti uses the similes 'He wore me like a silken knot, / He changed me like a glove' to present the lord's treatment of women in Cousin Kate.
0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Both similes compare the speaker to objects — a knot and a glove — reducing her to something decorative and disposable (1 mark)
- 'Wore' and 'changed' suggest the lord treats women as accessories to be used and replaced at will (1 mark)
- 'Silken' implies superficial beauty and fragility — the relationship looked fine but had no substance (1 mark)
- Links to Rossetti's critique of Victorian patriarchy: women's value was determined by men, and they could be discarded without consequence (1 mark)

0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.text: Compare how inner conflict is presented in A Poison Tree and Cousin Kate. You should compare language, form and structure, and consider relevant contexts. [20 marks]
0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Analyses: Blake's allegorical, impersonal approach (the speaker as symbolic figure) vs Rossetti's personal, dramatic monologue voice. Both use regular rhyme (Blake AABB, Rossetti ABCB ballad) but for different effects — Blake's nursery-rhyme simplicity makes murder disturbing; Rossetti's folk-song form suits her story of betrayal. Both present anger that grows from being mistreated, but Blake's speaker is calculatedly destructive while Rossetti's is defiantly triumphant. Blake's critique of repression vs Rossetti's critique of gender inequality.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison, mostly descriptive.
Lower band (1-5): Limited engagement.

0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.text: Explore how Wordsworth uses the structure of blank verse to reinforce the theme of nature's power in the extract from The Prelude.
0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) creates a continuous, unbroken flow that mirrors the boy's rowing across the lake (1 mark)
- The lack of stanza breaks means the reader cannot pause — reflecting how the experience overwhelms the boy without respite (1 mark)
- The regular metre occasionally breaks down when the mountain appears, reflecting the disruption to the boy's composure (1 mark)
- Links to Wordsworth's Romantic belief that nature is a force greater than human understanding — the form cannot contain the experience (1 mark)

0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.text: How does Rossetti present the speaker's defiance in the final stanza of Cousin Kate? Consider how the son transforms 'shame' into 'pride.'
0fd24743-45e4-4737-ba2d-c17656fa4740.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. 'My fair-haired son, my shame, my pride' uses an oxymoronic pair — the illegitimate child is both a source of social disgrace and personal triumph. The speaker directly challenges Kate: 'Yet I've a gift you have not got.' In Victorian society, producing an heir was a woman's ultimate purpose — the speaker has achieved this while the 'respectable' wife has not. The defiant tone inverts the power dynamic: the outcast woman becomes the one with genuine power.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of the final stanza.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding of the twist.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.text: Compare how Owen uses half-rhyme in Exposure and Blake uses full rhyme in A Poison Tree. How does each poet's rhyme scheme reinforce their poem's message?
505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive comparison. Owen's half-rhymes ('knive us / nervous') deny satisfying resolution, mirroring soldiers' denied expectations and creating unease. Blake's AABB full rhymes create a nursery-rhyme simplicity that makes the dark content (murder through deceit) more disturbing — the innocent form conflicts with sinister meaning. Both poets use rhyme as a tool of meaning, not just decoration.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear comparison with some analysis of effect.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Identifies the difference but limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple observation.

505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.text: Analyse how enjambment is used differently in Poppies (Weir) and Exposure (Owen). Refer to specific examples.
505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- In Poppies, enjambment ('hoping to hear / your playground voice') creates a breathless, reaching quality — the mother's emotion overflows the line, reflecting her uncontrolled grief (1 mark)
- In Exposure, enjambment drags lines out, creating a heavy, exhausting rhythm that mirrors the soldiers' endless waiting in the trenches (1 mark)
- Both use enjambment to reflect emotional states, but Weir's is active (reaching out) while Owen's is passive (enduring) (1 mark)
- This demonstrates that the same technique creates different effects depending on context and intention (1 mark)

505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.text: How does the use of non-standard English in Half-caste, No Problem and The Class Game function as an act of resistance? Compare at least two poems. [20 marks]
505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. All three poets refuse to adopt 'standard' English, which is itself a political statement: accepting the rules of a culture that marginalises you means accepting your marginalisation. Agard's Caribbean dialect and lack of punctuation reject the conventions of the culture that labelled him 'half-caste.' Casey's working-class voice rejects the idea that 'proper' speech equals intelligence. Zephaniah's dub rhythm connects his poetry to Jamaican oral tradition. each poet's cultural background shapes their linguistic choices.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison, basic observations.
Lower band (1-5): Limited engagement.

505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.text: Explain how caesura is used in Belfast Confetti and Exposure. What different effects does it create in each poem?
505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- In Belfast Confetti, dashes and full stops interrupt the speaker's thoughts mid-sentence, mimicking how violence disrupts normal thinking (1 mark)
- In Exposure, 'But nothing happens.' ends stanzas with a crushing, final pause that emphasises futility and hopelessness (1 mark)
- Carson's caesura creates confusion and disorder; Owen's creates resignation and defeat (1 mark)
- Both show how punctuation can be used structurally to convey psychological states — chaos in Carson, despair in Owen (1 mark)

505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.text: Why is Wordsworth's choice of blank verse significant for the extract from The Prelude? How does the form relate to the poem's content?
505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) creates a continuous, elevated tone appropriate for a profound spiritual experience. The absence of rhyme prevents predictable resolution, mirroring the boy's inability to process what he has witnessed. The lack of stanza breaks creates an unbroken flow that mirrors the boy's continuous rowing and the mountain's relentless advance. The regular metre occasionally falters when the mountain appears, reflecting the disruption to the boy's composure.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of blank verse with some effect.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Basic identification of blank verse.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.text: How does Tennyson's use of repetition in The Charge of the Light Brigade create the feeling of being surrounded by danger? Refer to specific examples.
505aa2d2-ce0a-4394-8967-a1d9a31f9203.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- 'Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them, / Cannon in front of them' uses anaphora to surround the reader with the word 'cannon', just as the soldiers were surrounded (1 mark)
- 'Valley of Death' is repeated throughout, creating a sense of inescapable doom — they are trapped (1 mark)
- The triple repetition mirrors the three directions of enemy fire, making the danger feel overwhelming (1 mark)
- The driving rhythm means these repeated phrases feel relentless, like the bombardment itself (1 mark)

df2a11c2-ecee-40ff-8b5b-da436171be1f.text: Analyse how Owen uses personification of nature in Exposure to convey the suffering of soldiers. Refer to the quote: 'merciless iced east winds that knive us.'
df2a11c2-ecee-40ff-8b5b-da436171be1f.marks:

- Connects to Owen's wider message about the futility of war — soldiers are not even dying in battle but from exposure to the elements (1 mark)

df2a11c2-ecee-40ff-8b5b-da436171be1f.text: How does Tennyson use repetition and rhythm in The Charge of the Light Brigade to convey the experience of the cavalry charge? Refer to specific examples.
df2a11c2-ecee-40ff-8b5b-da436171be1f.marks:

The anaphora of 'Cannon to right / left / front of them' surrounds the reader with danger. 'Valley of Death' is a biblical allusion (Psalm 23) elevating the soldiers' suffering to a spiritual trial. The shift from 'rode the six hundred' to 'left of six hundred' in the final stanzas quantifies the human cost.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of rhythm and repetition with effect on reader.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some identification of repetition with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple description of the poem's content.

df2a11c2-ecee-40ff-8b5b-da436171be1f.text: How does Hardy present the speaker's attitude towards killing in The Man He Killed? You should consider language, form and structure.

The hypothetical 'Had he and I but met / By some old ancient inn' humanises the enemy and exposes the arbitrariness of war.

df2a11c2-ecee-40ff-8b5b-da436171be1f.text: Compare how the reality of war is presented in Exposure and The Charge of the Light Brigade. You should compare the poets' use of language, form and structure, and consider relevant contexts. [20 marks]

df2a11c2-ecee-40ff-8b5b-da436171be1f.text: Explore how Owen uses form and structure in Exposure to reinforce the theme of futility. You should consider the whole poem.

df2a11c2-ecee-40ff-8b5b-da436171be1f.text: How does Tennyson present conflicting attitudes towards military command in The Charge of the Light Brigade? Refer to the line 'Someone had blundered.'

- Links to context — Tennyson was responding to a real event and balancing patriotic duty with honest reporting of incompetence (1 mark)

5d00f939-f7b6-4c71-8346-125758700059.text: Analyse how Weir uses the phrase 'playground voice catching on the wind' to convey the mother's grief in Poppies.
5d00f939-f7b6-4c71-8346-125758700059.marks:

5d00f939-f7b6-4c71-8346-125758700059.text: How does Levertov use the Q&A structure in What Were They Like? to present the destruction caused by war? Refer to specific examples.
5d00f939-f7b6-4c71-8346-125758700059.marks:

E.g. the numbered Q&A format resembles an anthropological survey about an extinct civilisation, which is deeply ironic because the Vietnamese were still alive when Levertov wrote it. The clinical tone of the questions contrasts with the increasingly emotional answers ('laughter is bitter to the burned mouth'). The past tense throughout treats the culture as already destroyed, forcing the reader to confront the finality of cultural erasure. The word 'Sir' in the answers is formally polite but accusatory.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of the Q&A structure with effect.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding of how structure conveys meaning.

5d00f939-f7b6-4c71-8346-125758700059.text: How does Weir present the relationship between the mother and son in Poppies? You should consider language, form and structure, and relevant context.

5d00f939-f7b6-4c71-8346-125758700059.text: Compare how the impact of war on those who did not fight is presented in Poppies and What Were They Like? You should compare language, form and structure, and consider relevant contexts. [20 marks]

5d00f939-f7b6-4c71-8346-125758700059.text: Analyse how Levertov uses the word 'Sir' in the answers section of What Were They Like? to convey her attitude towards those responsible for war.

ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.text: Compare how the poets present the connection between place and memory in 'Where the Picnic was' by Hardy and one other poem from the Time and Place collection.
ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison. For Hardy: pathetic fallacy ('winter mire'), symbolic objects ('stick-ends, charred'), short lines in shrinking stanzas. Compares with Jennings's unchanged garden, five-line stanzas, the 'savage force' of absence; or with Fanthorpe's spatial metaphor, shifting perspective. Explores how different forms create different emotional effects. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained. Mid band (7-9) Clear. Lower-mid band (4-6) Some. Lower band (1-3) Simple.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Perceptive — Hardy's preoccupation with mortality and Dorset landscapes; comparison poet's context. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some.

ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.text: Analyse how Hardy uses the landscape in 'Where the Picnic was' to convey the speaker's sense of loss.
ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of pathetic fallacy ('winter mire' reflecting emotional coldness), the charred sticks as a symbol of burned-out happiness, and the contrast between past warmth and present bleakness. Explores how the short lines and shrinking stanzas create a controlled, restrained tone that mirrors suppressed grief. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear analysis with examples. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some understanding. Lower band (1-2) Simple comment.

ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.text: How does Jennings use the unchanged garden in 'Absence' to explore the relationship between the speaker and the place?
ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of the sameness of the setting — well-tended gardens and steady fountains that carry on as if nothing had ended. Explores how that sameness sharpens the loss: 'It was because the place was just the same / That made your absence seem a savage force.' Discusses the three tight five-line stanzas compressing emotion. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear analysis. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some understanding. Lower band (1-2) Simple identification.

ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.text: Compare how the poets present departure or leaving in 'First Flight' by Fanthorpe and 'Adlestrop' by Thomas.
ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison. Fanthorpe: physical ascent, shrinking landscape, departure as loss of detail. Thomas: unexpected train stop, expansion outward from platform to counties, departure implied by the brevity of the moment. Both capture a transitional moment — arriving/leaving — but Thomas looks back at what was, while Fanthorpe looks down at what is disappearing. Form: Fanthorpe's expanding perspective vs Thomas's four tight quatrains. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained. Mid band (7-9) Clear.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Thomas writing in wartime about a vanished world; Fanthorpe's modern observation. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some.

ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.text: Explore how Fanthorpe uses the experience of flying for the first time to present the theme of loss in 'First Flight.'
ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of spatial distancing as emotional metaphor — familiar places shrink, details blur, the known world becomes abstract. Discusses how the shift in perspective (ground level to aerial) mirrors how memories fade when we leave a place. Gentle, melancholic tone rather than dramatic grief. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear analysis. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some understanding. Lower band (1-2) Simple comment.

ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.text: Compare how the poets present the idea that places are changed by human emotion in 'Absence' by Jennings and 'Where the Picnic was' by Hardy.
ac8dbc24-7b46-4ad6-964a-94e73bcfe5e5.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison. Jennings: the speaker's grief changes the place ('your absence seem a savage force'), an unchanged garden, five-line stanzas. Hardy: the landscape reflects the speaker's grief (pathetic fallacy, 'winter mire'), concrete symbols (charred sticks), short shrinking stanzas. Key difference: Jennings recognises projection; Hardy treats the landscape as naturally aligned with his sorrow. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained. Mid band (7-9) Clear.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Perceptive — Hardy's Victorian preoccupation with mortality; Jennings's Movement values of clarity and emotional honesty. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some.

2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.text: Compare how two poets from the Time and Place collection use poetic form to shape the reader's experience of place.
2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured analysis of form in both poems. Could compare Wordsworth's Petrarchan sonnet (octave/sestet, volta, association with admiration) with Alvi's uneven free-verse stanzas (jumping thought, no resolution). Or Keats's ode (three stanzas, sensory progression) with Afrika's clipped free verse (suppressed anger, fragmented lines). Explores how form reflects each poet's relationship to place. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained. Mid band (7-9) Clear. Lower-mid band (4-6) Some. Lower band (1-3) Simple.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Perceptive — links form choices to historical/literary context. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some.

2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.text: Analyse how Keats uses sensory language in the three stanzas of 'To Autumn' to create a sense of the season's progression.
2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of sensory progression — sight/touch (stanza 1: 'plump the hazel shells'), sight/stillness (stanza 2: figure on granary floor), sound (stanza 3: gnats, lambs, crickets). Explores how this progression mirrors autumn moving from abundance to decline. Links to Keats's awareness of mortality. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some. Lower band (1-2) Simple.

2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.text: How do Blake and Afrika use contrast within their poems to expose inequality? Compare their methods.
2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison. Blake: contrasts 'charter'd' control with cries of suffering, 'Marriage hearse' oxymoron. Afrika: contrasts restaurant ('linen falls, the single rose') with café ('plastic table's top'), white/non-white spaces. Both use place-based contrasts to reveal injustice, but Blake's are abstract/symbolic while Afrika's are concrete/physical. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained. Mid band (7-9) Clear.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Blake's 18th-century radical politics vs Afrika's post-apartheid anger. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some.

2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.text: Explore how structural features (such as stanza form, line length or repetition) create meaning in one poem from the Time and Place collection.
2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of structural features in a chosen poem. For example: Blake's anaphora of 'every' creating universality, tight quatrains containing rage; or Thomas's four quatrains expanding from platform to counties; or Dickinson's hymn metre contrasting with disturbing content. Explains how structure reinforces theme. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear analysis. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some understanding. Lower band (1-2) Simple identification.

2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.text: Compare how two poets use personification to present place in the Time and Place anthology.
2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison. Could compare Wordsworth (city 'wears' beauty 'like a garment,' houses 'seem asleep' — personification makes city feel part of nature) with Dickinson (sea as 'He' — personification creates threat and pursuit). Or Keats (Autumn as a human figure — creates intimacy and warmth). Explores how different personifications create different relationships between speaker and place. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained. Mid band (7-9) Clear.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Links personification to each poet's cultural/literary context. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some.

2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.text: Analyse how sound devices (such as alliteration, sibilance or assonance) contribute to the presentation of place in 'To Autumn' by Keats.
2ab3ecfb-3015-413d-8688-5e7bf612e347.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness' (sibilance and soft consonants creating drowsy warmth), 'And full-grown lambs loud bleat' (harder consonants in stanza 3 marking seasonal change). Explains how sound creates atmosphere and mirrors the sensory experience of place. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some. Lower band (1-2) Simple identification.

3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.text: Compare how Blakemore and Dharker present different ideas about what 'home' means. You should consider the poets' use of language, form and structure, as well as the contexts in which the poems were written. [20 marks]
3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive comparison. Analyses Blakemore's sensory accumulation celebrating physical place against Dharker's humorous exploration of imagined belonging. Explores form: Blakemore's listing vs Dharker's conversational tone. multicultural London vs Dharker's multilayered cultural identity.
Top band (13-16): Sustained comparison with clear analysis and some context.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.text: How does Kunial use the word 'us' to explore ideas about belonging and exclusion? [10 marks]
3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.marks:
Top band (9-10) Perceptive analysis. Explores the dual meaning of 'us' (inclusive and exclusive), wordplay and ambiguity, the Midlands 'us' that means 'me', the football crowd's 'we or us', the 'separations of us'. Kunial's Kashmiri-English heritage as background.
Top band (7-8): Sustained analysis with clear understanding.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear explanation with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some supported points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comment.

3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.text: Analyse how Blakemore uses accumulation to present Peckham Rye Lane as a place of belonging.
3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Identifies accumulation — piling up sensory details one after another (1 mark)
- Explains this creates an immersive effect, as though the reader is walking through the street (1 mark)
- Analyses how the technique conveys richness and cultural diversity as sources of belonging (1 mark)
- Links to context: Peckham as one of London's most diverse areas, where belonging is built from everyday multicultural life (1 mark)

3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.text: Compare how hybrid identity is presented in 'Us' and one other poem from the Belonging collection. [20 marks]
3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.marks:
Top band (17-20) Perceptive, sustained comparison. Analyses Kunial's linguistic exploration of the pronoun 'us' alongside chosen poem's presentation of hybrid identity. Integrates AO3 context for both poets. Explores similarities and differences.
Top band (13-16): Developed comparison with clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments.

3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.text: How does Dharker use humour to explore displacement in 'In Wales, Wanting to be Italian'?
3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Identifies the humour in the title's absurd juxtaposition — being in Wales but longing for Italy (1 mark)
- Explains that the self-deprecating tone makes displacement seem manageable rather than tragic (1 mark)
- Analyses how humour reveals the speaker's awareness that belonging is partly a matter of desire and imagination (1 mark)
- Links to Dharker's wider context: a life lived across multiple countries, where fixed identity is impossible (1 mark)

3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.text: Explore how the form and structure of 'Peckham Rye Lane' reinforce the poem's celebration of urban diversity. [10 marks]
3035834a-08af-4dd1-8658-4d4e1be8def6.marks:
Top band (9-10) Perceptive analysis. Explores accumulative structure as mirroring crowded street, listing technique as conveying overwhelming sensory richness, how the poem's energy reflects Peckham's vitality. contemporary multicultural Britain.
Top band (7-8): Sustained analysis with clear understanding.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear explanation.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some supported points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comment.

b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.text: Compare how the poets present places of suffering or oppression in 'London' by Blake and one other poem from the Time and Place collection.
b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparative analysis. For Blake: 'charter'd' (control), anaphora of 'every' (universality), 'mind-forg'd manacles' (psychological oppression), oxymoron 'Marriage hearse.' Compares with Afrika's physical/bodily language, clipped stanzas, contrast between restaurant and café. Explores how different forms create different kinds of anger — prophetic vs personal. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained comparison. Mid band (7-9) Clear comparison. Lower-mid band (4-6) Some comparison. Lower band (1-3) Simple comment.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Perceptive — Blake's radical politics and opposition to Church/monarchy; apartheid and District Six for Afrika. Upper-mid band (4) Clear context. Mid band (3) Some context.

b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.text: Analyse how Blake uses repetition in 'London' to convey the extent of suffering. Use examples from the poem.
b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of anaphora ('In every cry of every Man / In every Infant's cry'), repetition of 'charter'd,' and 'marks.' Explores how repetition creates a sense of inescapable, universal suffering. Links to Blake's political message about institutional oppression. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear analysis with examples. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some understanding. Lower band (1-2) Simple identification.

b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.text: How does Afrika use physical and sensory language in 'Nothing's Changed' to convey the speaker's anger?
b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of bodily language — 'my feet know,' 'my hands,' 'the hot, white, inwards turning / anger of my eyes.' Explores how the body remembers injustice before the mind processes it. Discusses the final image of wanting to smash glass as physical expression of rage. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear analysis. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some understanding. Lower band (1-2) Simple comment.

b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.text: Compare how the poets present the relationship between humans and their environment in 'Nothing's Changed' by Afrika and 'In Romney Marsh' by Davidson.
b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison. Afrika's environment is shaped by human injustice (bulldozed neighbourhood, segregated dining); Davidson's is indifferent to humans (vast sea, wind, stars). Afrika uses clipped, angry syntax; Davidson uses hymn-like quatrains and extended organ metaphor. Both speakers feel small in their landscapes but for opposite reasons. Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained comparison. Mid band (7-9) Clear comparison.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Perceptive — apartheid history vs late-Victorian response to nature. Upper-mid band (4) Clear. Mid band (3) Some.

b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.text: Explore how Davidson uses the extended metaphor of a cathedral organ in 'In Romney Marsh' to present the power of the natural landscape.
b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.marks: Top band (7-8) Perceptive analysis of 'organ stops / Pealing again, prolonged the roar' — the sea as a sacred instrument, nature as grand and inhuman. Discusses how the metaphor gives the landscape religious authority, making the speaker seem insignificant. Links to the hymn-like ABAB rhyme scheme reinforcing the worshipful tone. Upper-mid band (5-6) Clear analysis. Lower-mid band (3-4) Some understanding. Lower band (1-2) Simple identification.

b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.text: Compare how Blake in 'London' and Wordsworth in 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge' present the city of London. Consider the poets' different purposes and contexts.
b6562ab2-0b6d-49ac-8cbe-1e38f632b5a0.marks:
AO2 (15 marks): Top band (13-15) Assured comparison of contrasting visions of the same city. Blake: 'charter'd' streets, 'Marks of weakness,' prophetic anger. Wordsworth: 'Earth has not anything to show more fair,' sleeping city clothed in morning beauty. Explores how form (Blake's tight quatrains vs Wordsworth's Petrarchan sonnet) reinforces tone (anger vs admiration). Upper-mid band (10-12) Sustained. Mid band (7-9) Clear.
AO3 (5 marks): Top band (5) Perceptive — Blake's radical politics vs Wordsworth's Romantic idealism; different historical moments (1794 vs 1802); both Romantic poets with opposing views of the city.
